compute.anchor_note: Compute density per mm2 is derived from one published GPU's dense tensor roofs divided by its published whole-die area, then scaled by the node logic-density ratio. Applying a whole-die-derived density to a modelled design's COMPUTE-ONLY area is the model's stated compute assumption: it is conservative in that an A100 die spends area on HBM PHY, L2 and schedulers that the density is nevertheless charged for, and optimistic in that NVIDIA's tensor cores are a highly tuned datapath. Newer parts are denser: B200 achieves 2.81e12 FP8 ops/s/mm2 at 4NP against 1.50e12 predicted by scaling A100 INT8, so this anchor understates a 2026 design by roughly 1.9x.

bf16.note: A100 80GB SXM, 312 TFLOPS dense BF16 tensor (624 with structured sparsity, not used)

fp4.note: A100 publishes 1248 TOPS dense INT4; FP4 e2m1 is taken as the same datapath area as INT4

fp8.note: A100 publishes 624 TOPS dense INT8. An FP8 e4m3 multiply-accumulate is taken as the same datapath area as INT8; A100 itself has no FP8 unit, so this is a density transfer, not a claim about Ampere.

w4a8_density_rule.note: A 4-bit-weight by 8-bit-activation multiply-accumulate is bounded below by the w8a8 datapath (no narrowing credit taken) and above by the w4a4 datapath. NVIDIA publishes both endpoints on one die, so the bracket is published and only the interpolation is a judgement. Both endpoints are also reported so the bracket, not the midpoint, is what the reader checks.

compute.note: fraction of the peak tensor roof a real decode kernel sustains, covering pipeline bubbles, tail effects and non-tensor interleave

expert_router_imbalance.note: Multiplier on the per-region sweep depth, applied ON TOP OF the expected busiest-region load rather than instead of it. This replaces efficiencies.expert_load_balance = 0.85, which was documented as carrying 'the sweep depth is set by the busiest region rather than the mean' while the code divided the MEAN engaged-region load by it. The busiest region is now computed explicitly (roofline.expected_max_region_load), and a single constant cannot stand in for it: the ratio of the busiest region to the mean runs from 1.0 at batch 1 to about 3.0 at batch 64. What is left for this parameter is the residual imbalance of a TRAINED router against the uniform-random draw the busiest-region statistic assumes. It is 1.0 -- the neutral value, which makes it inert -- because no trace exists to set it, and because a parameter must not take its value from the answer it is wanted to produce. The per-region sweep depth is exactly linear in it, so a trace showing a 1.3x hot-expert bias moves every per-region number by 1.3x.

The only derates applied are the sustained-fraction ones named above.

The study reports the underated ceiling alongside it because this derate moves the ROM answer directly.

hbm_j_per_byte.note: 13.11 pJ/bit = 104.88 pJ/byte at the HBM level on a shipping A100 40GB (N7, Perlmutter), measured by microbenchmark regression and published at SC'25. VERIFIER-CORRECTED, 3.36x UP from the 31.2 pJ/B this entry used to carry. The incumbent was O'Connor's HBM2-era DRAM-DEVICE-ONLY model figure; this one is measured and its boundary is the whole HBM path -- DRAM device, TSV, interposer, processor-side PHY and the memory controller (the paper's Fig. 1 caption states verbatim that 'memory controller energy is tabulated with HBM energy'). Scope is beyond-L2 only: the paper subtracts separately-extracted L1 and L2 parameters (its Eq. 8), so per-byte SM front-end and address-generation overheads cancel out of this number rather than hiding inside it. 65% of the A100 figure (8.47 of 13.11 pJ/bit) is CONTROL PLANE -- controllers, addresses, row decoders, tag lookups -- so charging a non-GPU memory subsystem a GPU's control plane is an extrapolation and the range must be swept, not asserted. The range is the spread across the paper's four measured parts (GH200 11.68, A100 13.11, MI250X GCD 13.64, MI300A 14.72 pJ/bit); it is NOT an uncertainty band for a non-GPU part. Two further costs this term does NOT carry and the model still does not charge: L1/L2 traversal (a further 6.30 pJ/bit on the A100 for streaming traffic, same paper) and the device's traffic-independent power (the same paper's Table 2 publishes P_const = 54 W for the A100, which is what power.clocked_idle_floor_w_per_device now carries).
hbm_j_per_byte.source: https://escholarship.org/content/qt6189368s/qt6189368s.pdf -- Measuring the Energy of Data Movement on Modern GPU Systems, SC 2025, doi:10.1145/3712285.3759815, Table 3

operand_delivery_j_per_byte.note: 0.23 pJ/byte to get one byte from the array that holds it to the arithmetic that consumes it, at a 7 nm-class node. This is the term docs/TECHNICAL_DIRECTION_RECOMMENDATION.md 0.11 named as missing: a Horowitz-class MAC energy is the ALU, not the cost of delivering its operands, and rom_read_j_per_byte's stated boundary stops at the macro output latch. VERIFIER-CORRECTED, 1.5x DOWN from the submitted 3.43e-13 -- the submitted wire constant used alpha x C x V^2 with alpha = 0.5 transitions/bit, which double-counts the transition: supply energy for one full 0->1->0 cycle is C*V^2, so energy per transition is (1/2)C*V^2 and the correct coefficient for random data is 0.25, not 0.5. The corrected form is anchored, not chosen: 0.25 x 0.2 pF/mm x (0.75 V)^2 x 1.6 repeater overhead = 0.045 pJ/bit/mm, and the same formula run at 45 nm/1.0 V returns 0.080 pJ/bit/mm against Dally's published 45 nm figure of 6 pJ to move 64 bits 1 mm = 0.094 pJ/bit/mm, an 18% agreement the submitted form missed by 1.7x. Point = one register-file/operand-collector access at N7 (0.091 pJ/B, Horowitz 45 nm scaled by 5.49x) + 0.40 pJ/B/mm over a 0.35 mm tile pitch. BOUNDARY, and the writer must not lose it: this scalar is the TILE-LOCAL FLOOR. The long-path ladder -- HBM to L2 to register file on an A100 is 8.3-10.0 pJ/B over 10-14.4 mm -- is NOT represented. Applied uniformly to weight and KV bytes it charges the ROM side ~1.6x on its dominant term and the GPU side ~1.01x on its dominant term, so the single number penalises the ROM side; that is the safe direction and it is why a scalar is shippable. The 5.49x 45nm->N7 node factor is the geometric mean of ratios implied by this file's own mac_energy_j_per_op entries, every one of which is graded `assumed`: an assumption resting on assumptions, and SRAM energy scales worse than logic, so if anything this understates the storage-level terms.
operand_delivery_j_per_byte.source: Horowitz, Computing's Energy Problem, ISSCC 2014 (register-file and cache access energies at 45 nm) ; Dally, published 45 nm wire energy, 64 bits x 1 mm = 6 pJ ; repeatered global wire C ~= 0.2 pF/mm at a leading node. NOT sourced to Sze et al. arXiv:1703.09039: that paper's Fig. 22 is NORMALISED ONLY (ALU 1x, RF 1x, NoC 2x, buffer 6x, DRAM 200x) and contains no pJ figure, so it cannot support any absolute constant and the earlier citation of it was a misreading.

rom_read_j_per_byte.note: 0.08 pJ/byte at N6 for the ROM read primitive -- address decode, wordline, bitline develop, sense/sample and macro output latch -- excluding the arithmetic, which roofline.py charges separately as mac_energy_j_per_op. VERIFIER-CORRECTED grade, not value: submitted as `derived` at 8e-14 and REGRADED to `assumed`, because the derivation behind it did not survive. It rests on the geometric centre of two methods that disagree by ~5x over a 17x-wide bracket (~0.02 to ~0.35 pJ/B), which is a point estimate, not a derivation. What the bracket is built from: (a) six published ROM/compute-in-ROM macros' TOPS/W scaled by node and V^2 -- but at most THREE of the six are fabricated silicon (BitROM is post-layout, YOLoC is SPICE with peripherals estimated from a different paper and publishes NO supply voltage at all, DCiROM claims no measurement), and a CiM macro's TOPS/W includes the arithmetic this boundary excludes, so that method measures something strictly LARGER than the term; (b) a 130 nm mask-ROM tile read of 1.20 pJ per sensed ternary weight = 4.80 pJ/B, scaled by (0.75/1.80)^2 and by a cell-to-cell area ratio of 14.3, giving ~0.02-0.09 pJ/B at N6. THE DIRECTION MATTERS: this is 6.25x BELOW the 0.5 pJ/byte this entry used to carry, so adopting it makes the Taalas HC1 power gate WORSE, not better. It is adopted anyway because the evidence points there. The 0.5 pJ/B it replaces was a schema default with no evidence at all.
rom_read_j_per_byte.source: Yin et al., JSSC 2023 and JSSC 2025 (doi:10.1109/JSSC.2025.3556008); Cheong et al., A-SSCC 2024; YOLoC, GLSVLSI 2022 (doi:10.1145/3489517.3530576, simulated, supply voltage unpublished); BitROM, ASP-DAC 2026 (post-layout); Ankhdjet 130 nm mask-ROM tile read, arXiv:2608.26206 Table VII (1.20 pJ per ternary weight at tt/27C/1.80V). No fabricated leading-node mask-ROM macro reports read energy at the macro boundary separately from compute.

Shipping parts therefore use roughly 50-60% of the die edge for HBM, the rest going to host, scale-up and power. 0.60 is taken as the ceiling, which makes a modelled ROM part's HBM beachfront no more aggressive than NVIDIA's own. This matters: at equal die area both sides then have the SAME KV bandwidth ceiling, and the ROM part's advantage is only that it does not also spend that bandwidth on weights.

hbm.note: An HBM3 channel is split into two 32-bit pseudo-channels and the minimum burst is 8, so the smallest read that reaches the die is 32 bytes. A 68-byte index entry therefore costs 96 bytes. Graded assumed rather than published because the number is reconstructed from the interface geometry rather than read off a datasheet line.
hbm.source: HBM3/3E pseudo-channel width times burst length; no vendor erratum consulted for this program

sram.note: The row width a wide on-die SRAM macro delivers per access. 128 bytes is a common leading-node macro word for a bandwidth-optimised array; a narrower 64-byte macro halves the waste on a 68-byte entry only because 68 still spills into a second word. Sweep 64 to 256.
sram.source: no vendor macro datasheet for the target on-die arrays

index_layout.note: Where a compressed-sparse layer's 68-byte index entry sits relative to the 583-byte payload entry it describes. 'interleaved' is the natural result of writing both at generation time and makes every index entry its own access; 'contiguous' packs the index array separately so the scan is one sequential run and granule rounding costs nothing. The two differ by more than 1.6x on DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 200K context, where 72% of the KV read is that scan. Stated as a named choice because a design can simply choose the cheap one -- and because a model that silently assumed the cheap one would be claiming a design decision as a fact.
index_layout.source: layout CHOICE, not a physical constant; no released serving implementation inspected for this program

kv.purpose: How KV bytes are actually moved, as opposed to how many the algorithm needs. workload.kv_traffic counts algorithmic bytes; a memory system moves whole granules, and for a sparse-index model most of the KV read is a scan of entries far smaller than one granule.

array_pass_boundaries_per_layer.note: Serially dependent matrix passes in one decoder layer. Four is the standard block; a fused QKV gives three and a separate router pass gives five. Graded assumed rather than derived because the model profiles do not state a pass structure -- operations.operation_inventory counts arithmetic, not passes.
array_pass_boundaries_per_layer.source: transformer block structure: QKV, attention output, gate/up, down

global_wire_delay_s_per_mm.note: 100-250 ps/mm is the commonly quoted range for an optimally repeatered global interconnect at 7 nm class; it is flat with scaling because repeater insertion linearises RC. The traversal DISTANCE is derived from the floorplan rather than assumed: sqrt(reticle.area_mm2), which is one die edge, taken as the mean distance an activation broadcast covers. Charged once per array-pass boundary and once for the KV round trip.
global_wire_delay_s_per_mm.source: repeatered global-wire delay per millimetre at a leading node

layer_barrier_s.note: A layer transition is a barrier: every lane's partial result must be retired and the residual formed before the next layer's activation exists. On a distributed fabric this is a reduction plus a broadcast of the completion signal, on top of the wire delay charged separately. Charged once per layer.
layer_barrier_s.source: no published synchronisation cost for this class of part

pipeline_fill_drain_s.note: Fill and drain across the boundary between two SERIALLY DEPENDENT array passes. The second pass cannot begin until the first has retired, so the boundary costs a full traversal of the pipeline. 32 ns is roughly 32 stages at a 1 GHz fabric clock; the low end is a shallow accumulator tree over 4k lanes (12-16 levels) and the high end is a systolic drain of a 128-deep array. Charged once per array-pass boundary. THIS IS THE LARGEST TERM IN THE BLOCK and the widest band; the anchor is reported at both ends of it.
pipeline_fill_drain_s.source: no published array pipeline depth for this class of part

latency.purpose: The serial per-layer cost that no amount of bandwidth removes. Before this block the only latency in the model was links.*.hop_latency_s, charged at inter-partition boundaries, so a single_chip design had a decode step with no fixed cost at all. EVERY TERM HERE IS DERIVED FROM A PRIMITIVE THAT EXISTS INDEPENDENTLY OF THE TAALAS HC1 ANCHOR, and each carries range_low/range_high. The anchor gate is evaluated at both ends of that band and reports where it lands as an OUTCOME. No term is chosen to close the anchor gap: doing that would turn a validation gate into a one-parameter curve fit, and the gate is load-bearing (checklist W12.5). Charged per layer: sequencer_issue_decode + layer_barrier + one KV round trip (sram_access + one global traversal) + array_pass_boundaries_per_layer x (pipeline_fill_drain + one global traversal). Compressed-sparse layers additionally pay sparse_index_dependency.

sequencer_issue_decode_s.note: Instruction fetch, decode and operand setup for one layer's command stream in a statically scheduled sequencer. A few cycles at a ~1 GHz fabric clock; 1-8 ns spans a single-cycle issue to a deeply decoded microcoded one. Charged once per layer.
sequencer_issue_decode_s.source: no published sequencer for a mask-ROM or compute-in-ROM inference die

sparse_index_dependency_s.note: Charged only on layers whose profile says compressed_sparse. The gather address is not known until the index scan's top-k has completed, so the layer pays a selection over tens of thousands of candidates followed by a round trip that cannot be prefetched. 128 ns sits above an SRAM round trip and below a DRAM row cycle, which is the bracket a top-k-then-gather falls in. The bytes of the scan itself are charged against bandwidth, with their access granularity, in the kv block.
sparse_index_dependency_s.source: no published top-k selection pipeline at this candidate count

sram_access_s.note: Access time of a large on-die SRAM macro: address decode, wordline rise, bitline develop, sense and output latch. 1-4 ns brackets the published range for bandwidth-optimised leading-node macros of the size this model places. Charged once per layer, as the read half of the KV round trip; the KV BYTES are charged separately against bandwidth and this is only the dependency bandwidth cannot overlap.
sram_access_s.source: no vendor macro datasheet for the target on-die arrays

hop_latency_s.note: Cerebras publishes no SwarmX latency figure, and the one adjacent figure it does publish is a bound rather than a measurement: the Hot Chips 2024 CS-3 slide reads "Latency: CS-3 IO is <5us / 4 hops required", over RDMA over Ethernet. Read per hop that lands exactly on the 5.0 us stated here; read as the whole four-hop path it would be 1.25 us and would move the headline sharply in this study's favour. A slide bullet cannot be disambiguated and a vendor bound is not a third-party measurement, so the value is unchanged and the slide is recorded only as the reason the previous sentence -- "no SwarmX latency figure in any form" -- was too strong. SwarmX is a broadcast-reduce tree over 100 GbE, so the class of the link is known even where the number is not: 100 GbE RDMA between accelerator buffers is the same 3.7-5.7 us class the InfiniBand measurements give, and 5.0 us is taken as the point. The low end of the sweep, 1.0 us, is a purpose-built wafer-to-wafer link better than anything shipping; the high end, 10.0 us, is a tree with a second level. This is the number that decides whether a twelve-wafer machine is one machine or twelve, and this study previously charged it the on-wafer stitched-mesh hop of 100 ns -- the ROM-side mirror of charging a GPU cluster a 672-way pipeline.

hop_latency_s.note: WHAT THIS MODEL CHARGES A HOP FOR: one traversal of the NVSwitch tier. An A100 baseboard is a single all-to-all tier, so `collective_traversals` charges an in-domain all-reduce exactly two of them, and this model has no per-collective software term anywhere. This constant is therefore only ever consumed as 2 x hop = the WHOLE in-domain all-reduce at zero payload, and it has to be read as half a measured collective rather than as a wire delay. WITHDRAWN: the previous note's central claim, "NVIDIA publishes no NVLink or NVSwitch latency figure in any form -- six first-party pages were checked". NVIDIA does publish one, in the shipping source of its own collective library: NCCL's cost model carries hwLatencies[NVLINK][Ring][LL] = 0.6 us per NVLink ring step (src/tuning/cost_model.cc, byte-identical in v2.18.3-1 src/graph/tuning.cc), alongside 1.9 us for LL128 and 3.4 us for Simple, and NCCL's maintainer states the same three per-hop costs (about 1, 2 and 6 us) in NVIDIA's own issue tracker. A least-squares fit to a measured 2-to-8 GPU DGX A100 LL sweep gives 0.725 us per ring step on a 10.6 us fixed intercept, within 20% of NVIDIA's own constant. So the WIRE step is published and small; what a collective costs is set by a fixed software floor, and that floor is measured. WHAT IS MEASURED, at this model's granularity -- a whole 8-rank in-domain all-reduce at the smallest message, halved: best kernel 5.0 us, so 2.5 us per traversal (MSCCL++, ASPLOS 2026, 8x A100-40G over NVLink 3.0, 1 KB); MSCCL's all-pairs 9.5 us, so 4.75 us; stock NCCL 20.6 us, so 10.3 us. Four independent runs agree on the NCCL figure -- MSCCL++ Fig. 7 = 20.63 us; nccl-tests issue #149 on 8x A100-SXM4-80GB with NV12 between every pair = 20.65 us at 8 B and flat to 512 B; nccl-tests issue #123 on a DGX A100 with ALGO=Ring PROTO=LL = about 21 us; and NCCL's own cost model predicts 6.6 + 14 x 0.6 = 15.0 us. Point-to-point comparators, all third-party and all on fabricated A100 silicon: 3.65 us GPU-buffer to GPU-buffer through the six NVSwitches of a DGX A100 (Spetko et al., Energies 2021, Table 4 -- the same table measures 281.0 of the 300 GB/s this entry's `bytes_s` claims, so the bandwidth here is 6.8% optimistic too); 9.73 us one-way NCCL on two A100s (De Sensi et al. SC24 artifact, Zenodo 13312325); 10.4-13.5 us OSU MPI device-to-device on Polaris and Perlmutter (Siefert et al., SC-W 2023). STATED AT 2.5 us -- the best measured small-message all-reduce on this exact hardware, divided by the two traversals this model charges. It is the GPU-side twin of how `links.on_wafer` is now set: both sides are priced at the best measured kernel for their fabric, and both notes record that the library each vendor actually ships is 2-4x worse. The previous 1.5 us was BELOW every A100 measurement in existence -- it implies a 3.0 us in-domain all-reduce where the best measured is 5.0 us and the production stack measures 20.6 us -- so it flattered the GPU. Correcting it moves the headline UP, which is the direction that deserves the most suspicion, and is why the point is pinned to the best kernel rather than to NCCL. THE BAND. LOW 1.0 us is a 2.0 us in-domain all-reduce: below the 2.37 us best device-initiated kernel measured on GB200, which is a two-generation newer fabric, and above the 1.404 us speed-of-light floor those authors compute for it. That floor is 2 x 0.306 us L2 round trip + 0.792 us remote store; the previous note quoted the two terms as if they summed to 1.404 and they sum to 1.098, and only ONE of the three terms crosses the interconnect at all. LOW is deliberately GPU-favouring. HIGH 10.3 us is stock NCCL measured on this part, folded into the hop because the model has no term for a collective's fixed software cost. The measured spread of that cost for one nominal operation across production A100 and MI250X systems is 0.65 us to 32.8 us, and two machines with the same GPU SKU and the same GPU-GPU interconnect differ by 2.2x on the same benchmark, so what this band reports is the software stack and not the link. NOT ADOPTED: 9.73 us one-way NCCL point-to-point, which is the single best-established number in the evidence -- checksummed artifact, benchmark source read, halving convention confirmed at pp_Nccl.cu:358. Leonardo is a 4-GPU direct-connect node with no NVSwitch, and the figure carries NCCL's whole per-collective software cost inside a constant this model defines per traversal. It sits inside the band instead.

hop_latency_s.note: WHAT THIS MODEL CHARGES A HOP FOR: one traversal of the NVLink 5 switch tier. The domain is a single all-to-all tier, so `collective_traversals` charges an in-domain all-reduce exactly two of them and nothing else; with no per-collective software term anywhere in this model, 2 x hop IS the whole in-domain all-reduce at zero payload. The constant is half a measured collective, not a wire delay. WITHDRAWN: the previous note's claim that "NVIDIA publishes no NVLink or NVSwitch latency figure in any form". NCCL's shipping source states 0.6 us per NVLink ring step for the LL protocol (src/tuning/cost_model.cc), which is a first-party per-traversal figure; the previous note's arithmetic was also wrong, quoting the speed-of-light floor as "0.306 us L2 round trip plus 0.792 us remote store" when those sum to 1.098 and the published formula is 2 x L2 round trip + remote store = 1.404 us, of which only the remote store crosses the interconnect. WHAT IS MEASURED, on the Blackwell fabric this entry prices: on a GB200 NVL72 the speed-of-light all-reduce floor is 1.404 us; the best device-initiated low-latency kernel achieves 2.37 us for a small message on 4 GB200; and stock NCCL's ring costs 11.0 us for the same operation (Shen, Korzh, Bachan et al., arXiv:2607.16100, with NCCL's own maintainer as a co-author). The same paper states verbatim that a single-tier all-reduce's latency is "independent of the number of ranks involved", which is the published warrant for the two-traversal rule this constant is multiplied by. STATED AT 1.2 us -- the 2.37 us best measured kernel divided by the two traversals this model charges. That is BELOW the 1.5 us previously assumed, so re-grading made the GPU side faster and moved the headline against the side this study argues for. THE BAND. LOW 0.7 us is the measured speed-of-light floor halved, which is a hardware bound nothing can beat. HIGH 5.5 us is stock NCCL's measured ring halved, folded into the hop because the model has no term for a collective's fixed software cost. The A100 twin of this entry, `links.nvlink3`, carries the full measurement list and the A100-generation numbers; the two are set by the same rule -- best measured kernel for the point, hardware floor and shipped library for the ends -- so that the two studies price their GPUs the same way.

bytes_s.note: 26.75 PB/s, AND IT IS THE N5 PART'S FIGURE CHARGED AT N7, DELIBERATELY. Cerebras' own documents disagree on the unit -- the CS-3 cluster datasheet says 214 PB/s core-to-core and the WSE-2 weight-streaming paper says 220 Pb/s -- and 214 Pb/s is exactly 26.75 PB/s. This model takes the bit reading, which is eight times the more conservative of the two and is therefore the reading that does NOT flatter the wafer. The 2026-08-31 node audit found a second, smaller mismatch inside that: 214 Pbit/s is WSE-3's published fabric bandwidth (Hot Chips 36, 2024) while THIS entry prices the N7 generation, whose own published figure is 220 Pbit/s = 27.5 PB/s -- the 7nm part is 2.8% FASTER on this term, because it clocks 850,000 cores at a published 1.1 GHz against WSE-3's 900,000 at about 1.0. The value is left at the lower N5 number rather than raised to WSE-2's own, because the difference is a 3% disagreement between two vendor documents on a term that binds no design in either study, and taking it would move a headline in this study's favour. It is an under-credit to the N7 wafer fabric and it is recorded as one.

hop_latency_s.note: THIS IS THE N7-GENERATION ENTRY; ITS N5 TWIN IS `links.on_wafer_n5`. Until 2026-08-31 one wafer constant served BOTH studies while the GPU side already had two -- `nvlink3` at 2.5 us for the A100/N7 study, `nvlink5` at 1.2 us for the B200/4NP study -- so the N5/4NP study was charging the ROM side a 7nm-era wafer fabric against a 4nm-era NVLink. The split is now made; the N5 entry carries the WSE-3 derivation and the reason it lands on the SAME 125 ns, which is that the N7-to-N5 shrink went into the core rather than into the distance between cores and the clock did not move. Both sides of this comparison now scale with their node, or are stated equal for a reason. THE REST OF THIS NOTE IS THE N7 DERIVATION. WHAT THIS MODEL CHARGES A HOP FOR: one step between adjacent 815 mm2 reticle fields -- `reticle.area_mm2`, a 28.55 mm square -- of which one wafer holds 57. It is NOT a tile-to-tile hop and NOT a scribe-line crossing, and confusing them is a factor of 125: the single clock cycle Cerebras publishes is a hop between adjacent cores about 0.23 mm apart, and there are about 126 of those across one of this model's fields. Substituting the published one-cycle figure straight into this entry would give about 1.2 ns and would take the headline iso-area ratio from 8.33x to 14.7x. WHAT THE SOURCES MEASURE. (1) One cycle per core-to-core hop, ROUTER INCLUDED, is vendor-published for a shipping part -- WSE-3 white paper, "Each router uses lossless flow control with low buffering. This design enables single clock cycle latency between nodes"; Hot Chips 34, "Single cycle latency between cores" -- and independently stated on fabricated silicon by four peer-reviewed groups (Rocki SC20, Orenes-Vera ICS 2023, Luczynski HPDC 2024, Santos SC24). (2) Cerebras publishes the core grid outright at Hot Chips 34: die "17mm x 30mm", "66 x 154 Cores", core "228um x 170um", wafer "215mm x 215mm", "12 x 7 Die". (3) The clock is 850 MHz on every CS-2 in the literature and 1.1 GHz at Cerebras' stated design point. Cerebras publishes NO latency for the stitched reticle boundary itself in any document -- every vendor claim about it is about bandwidth or uniformity -- so the boundary is taken as one ordinary hop, which the end-to-end results below bound at no more than a few cycles. THE CONVERSION, stated so it can be checked: a field crossing costs (28.55 mm / core pitch) cycles / clock. WSE-2 at the published 0.224 mm geometric-mean pitch is 127 hops = 116 ns at 1.1 GHz to 150 ns at 850 MHz; WSE-3's geometry is not published at all -- see `links.on_wafer_n5`, where three published-input estimators put it at 126-131 hops against this 127, i.e. equal to within the method's resolution and if anything slower; CS-1 at the 89 x 51 tile grid Rocki publishes (0.348 mm) is 82 hops = 75-97 ns. Two MEASURED end-to-end results land inside that band. Rocki's full-wafer scalar AllReduce over about 380,000 processors takes "under 1.5 microseconds", which through this model's own 15.4 traversals at span 57 is at most 97 ns per field crossing. Santos et al. (SC24) state a wafer edge-to-edge latency "of around a microsecond", which the published geometry reproduces without adjustment (7 x 154 = 1,078 hops at 850 MHz = 1.27 us). The closest granularity match in existence is not Cerebras at all: Tesla publishes "100ns die-to-die latency" for a 645 mm2 reticle-class D1 die crossing to its neighbour inside a wafer-scale training tile (Hot Chips 34), and its own-die traversal scaled to 815 mm2 adds about 11 ns, so a bonded reticle-to-reticle step is about 111 ns. STATED AT 125 ns: the middle of the two N7 routes -- Dojo 111 ns bonded, Cerebras 116-150 ns stitched -- which is the node this entry prices. That is 25% ABOVE the 100 ns this entry previously assumed, so re-grading moved the constant AGAINST the side this study argues for. THE BAND, 75-250 ns, both ends evidenced rather than guessed. LOW is the coarsest tile pitch any wafer-scale part has shipped (CS-1's 0.348 mm, Rocki Fig. 2) at the fastest clock any vendor has published (1.1 GHz) -- and it is a real possibility rather than a formality, because a ROM region is a mask-ROM array and not a 38,000 um2 processing element, so a purpose-built design may legitimately put fewer routers across the same millimetres. Latency across a fixed distance is (distance / router pitch) x (1 cycle), so router pitch is the design choice this constant really encodes. HIGH is NOT a slower wire: it is the same wire under the collective the vendor SDK actually ships. Luczynski et al. measure Cerebras' own library running a corner-rooted X-Y AllReduce whose path is about 2x the mesh diameter, against the 1.1x diameter Rocki's hand-written kernel achieves and `MESH_ALLREDUCE_DIAMETER_FACTOR` charges; that 1.8x on the traversal count, folded into the hop because the model has no term for the collective algorithm, is about 230 ns, plus their measured 62-146 ns per-collective fixed floor which the model also has no term for. RETIRED: the previous 30-500 ns sweep. 30 ns requires 1.05 ns/mm, three times faster than the fastest axis any wafer-scale part has ever shipped; 500 ns is above every measurement in the literature. WITHDRAWN: the previous note's cross-check, "about 73 tiles across one 815 mm2 reticle field, so a reticle crossing is on the order of 73 cycles". It does not reproduce -- 900,000 cores over 46,225 mm2 is 15,868 cores in 815 mm2 and sqrt(15,868) = 126, not 73. The error was 1.7x and it ran in this study's favour.

hop_latency_s.note: THE N5 TWIN OF `links.on_wafer`, AND A NULL RESULT. This entry exists because one wafer-fabric constant was serving BOTH studies while the GPU side already had two -- `nvlink3` at 2.5 us for the A100/N7 study and `nvlink5` at 1.2 us for the B200/4NP study. `on_wafer` is derived from Cerebras WSE-2, a TSMC 7nm part, so the N6/N7 study was matched and the N5/4NP study was not: it charged the ROM side a 7nm-era wafer fabric against a 4nm-era NVLink, which understates the ROM side in exactly the study where it should be strongest. The wafer fabric is therefore node-keyed too, and this is the N5 entry, anchored on WSE-3 (TSMC 5nm, Hot Chips 2024). THE METHOD IS THE SAME ONE, DELIBERATELY -- two figures derived two ways are not comparable, which is the whole point of splitting the entry. A field crossing costs (28.55 mm / core pitch) cycles / clock, where 28.55 mm is sqrt(`reticle.area_mm2`), this model's reticle field edge, and the cycle is the vendor-published one-cycle core-to-core hop, router included. THE RESULT IS A NULL: N5 DOES NOT BUY A FASTER HOP, and this entry is therefore stated at the same 125 ns as its N7 twin. The method has exactly two terms and neither moved. (1) CORE PITCH DID NOT SHRINK. Cerebras publishes NO WSE-3 geometry. The Hot Chips 2024 successor to the WSE-2 slide that carried "17mm x 30mm", "66 x 154 Cores", "228um x 170um", "12 x 7 Die" and "215mm x 215mm" carries only three labels -- "10.7k Cores", "84 Die", "900k Cores" -- and every geometric dimension was dropped. What IS published bounds the pitch three ways, and all three land on or slightly ABOVE the N7 hop count of 127 per field: (a) the WSE-3 core is "approximately 38,000 um2 of silicon area in the TSMC 5 nm process" against WSE-2's published 228 x 170 = 38,760 um2, a 2.0% reduction, which at WSE-2's own fill fraction is 0.2218 mm of pitch and 129 hops; (b) 46,225 mm2 over the 900,000 ACTIVE cores is 0.2266 mm and 126 hops; (c) over the 970,000 PHYSICAL cores Cerebras states in its 2025 yield paper it is 0.2183 mm and 131 hops. The N7-to-N5 shrink went into the core, not into the distance between cores: the WSE-3 white paper gives the core the same 48 kB of SRAM, the same 110,000 standard cells and the same 50/50 logic-to-SRAM split as WSE-2, with the transistors spent on doubling the FP16 SIMD from 4-wide to 8-wide. Note the direction: a SMALLER core would make this constant WORSE. Latency across a fixed 28.55 mm is (distance / router pitch) x 1 cycle, so more routers per millimetre is more cycles per millimetre -- process scaling buys a mesh cores, not distance. (2) THE CLOCK DID NOT MOVE. Cerebras publishes 1.1 GHz for WSE-2 (Hot Chips 34, "Power efficient design point ... 1.1GHz clock frequency") and publishes NO WSE-3 clock in any document -- not the Hot Chips 36 deck, not the 2024 white paper, not the press release, not the product page. Two back-derivations from figures Cerebras DOES publish, each calibrated on WSE-2 where the answer is known, with every input stated so the arithmetic can be checked. MEMORY ROUTE, bandwidth / cores / the published 24 B per cycle SRAM port ("192-bit access per cycle from two 64-bit reads and one 64-bit write"): WSE-2 is 20 PB/s / 850,000 / 24 = 0.98 GHz against a published 1.1, so the method reads 1.12x low; WSE-3 is 21 PB/s / 900,000 / 24 = 0.97 GHz, or 1.00 GHz on the 21.6 PB/s the CS-4 datasheet's 43.2 PB/s implies for exactly half a WSE-3 Turbo -- corrected for the bias, 1.09 to 1.12 GHz. FABRIC ROUTE, bandwidth / cores / the published five-port router's 4 x 32-bit bidirectional interfaces (256 bit per cycle): WSE-2 is 220 Pbit/s / 850,000 / 256 = 1.01 GHz (bias 1.09x); WSE-3 is 214 Pbit/s / 900,000 / 256 = 0.93 GHz, corrected 1.01. So 1.01-1.12 GHz at N5 against 1.1 GHz published at N7: flat, inside a method whose own error on the calibration part is 9-12%. The 1.4 GHz that 2026 press reports quote for WSE-3 has NO vendor source -- it is a journalist's explicitly hedged inference ("I think", The Next Platform, 19 August 2026) back-read from the CS-4 launch -- and it is not used here. (3) THE BONDED ROUTE IS CHARGED AT BOTH NODES, WHICH IS THE CRUX. The N7 entry's 125 ns is the middle of TWO routes: Cerebras' stitched 116-150 ns and Tesla's bonded 111 ns, the latter from Dojo's published "100ns die-to-die latency" for a 645 mm2 reticle-class die inside a wafer-scale training tile, plus about 11 ns to scale its own-die traversal to 815 mm2 (Hot Chips 34, 2022). No bonded wafer-scale part has been published at N5. Withholding that route from the N5 entry -- which would put it at the stitched-only midpoint of about 132 ns and make N5 look WORSE than N7 -- would be applying a different method at the two nodes, and the whole reason for splitting this entry was that two figures derived two ways are not comparable. A bonded reticle interface is a packaging choice, not a property of the logic node, so it is offered to both. Both entries therefore blend the same two routes and differ only in the two node-dependent inputs above, neither of which moved. (4) WHAT THE NULL COSTS, STATED. 126-131 hops at N5 against 127 at N7 is -1% to +3% around the N7 figure, median estimator 1.6% SLOWER; the clock routes are flat to within their own bias. That is below the resolution of a method whose N7 input is itself rounded -- "17mm x 30mm" is a rounded 17.92 x 30.71, since 215/12 and 215/7 are what reproduce 46,225 exactly -- so the two nodes are stated EQUAL. Where the estimators do point they point SLOWER at N5, so stating them equal credits this study's own side by about 1.6% rather than costing it. Recorded here so it is not mistaken for a correction that went our way: a faster N5 wafer fabric would have RAISED the headline, and the evidence does not support one. THE STAKE, MEASURED: driving this entry alone to the low end of its own band, 75 ns, and re-simulating moves the N5 study's batch-1 headline from 5.85x to 8.03x and its DeepSeek-V4-Pro point at 554,700 mm2 from 4.01x to 5.00x, while leaving the N6 study unchanged to four decimals; driving `on_wafer` alone the same way moves N6 (10.78x to 13.95x) and leaves N5 unchanged. So the split is live and an N5-specific speed-up was worth up to 1.37x on that study's headline -- which is why it had to be derived rather than chosen. THE BAND, 75-250 ns, is the same as the N7 twin's and for the same two reasons, neither of which is a node argument. LOW is the coarsest tile pitch any wafer-scale part has shipped (CS-1's 0.348 mm, Rocki Fig. 2) at the fastest clock any vendor has published (1.1 GHz); it is a router-PITCH design choice, and a mask-ROM region is not a 38,000 um2 processing element, so a purpose-built design may legitimately put fewer routers across the same millimetres. HIGH is the same wire under the corner-rooted collective Cerebras' own SDK ships, which Luczynski et al. measure at about 2x the mesh diameter against the 1.1x `MESH_ALLREDUCE_DIAMETER_FACTOR` charges, plus their measured 62-146 ns per-collective fixed floor the model has no term for. NOT PUBLISHED AT EITHER NODE: the reticle-boundary crossing itself. For WSE-3 Cerebras states only that the fabric "crosses less than a millimeter of scribe line", that dies connect "at full performance" and that "software always sees a fully uniform 2D mesh" -- bandwidth and uniformity claims, never a latency. The boundary is taken as one ordinary hop at both nodes, which the end-to-end measurements cited on the N7 entry bound at no more than a few cycles.

clock_energy_j_per_mm2_per_cycle.note: 8.5e-11 J per mm2 per clock cycle for the clock network -- the distribution tree, its buffers and the clock pins it drives -- charged on every clocked mm2 whether or not a byte moves. VERIFIER-CORRECTED, 15% DOWN from the submitted 1.0e-10, which violated its own stated selection rule ('take the estimator that closes less of the gap' yields 8.48e-11 and the submission rounded up past it). WHAT THIS NUMBER ACTUALLY IS, and the note must say it plainly: clock distribution taken as 20-45% of a shipping NON-ANCHOR GPU's published TDP density, applied at that part's published clock. P100 is 300 W over 610 mm2 at 1480 MHz = 0.492 W/mm2 = 3.32e-10 J/mm2/cycle; GV100 is 300 W over 815 mm2 at 1530 MHz = 0.368 W/mm2 = 2.41e-10; 30% of each, geometric mean, is 8.5e-11. No node correction from 16FF+/12FFN to N7/N6 and no modern-clock-gating discount is applied, and the 20-45% band itself comes from 1992-2004 CPUs (Alpha 21064/21164, MCORE, XScale) with little fine-grain gating. THE SUBMITTED BOTTOM-UP ROUTE IS NOT A SECOND ESTIMATOR AND MUST NOT BE SOLD AS ONE: rebuilt on measured 7 nm primitives instead of its invented capacitance scaling (ASAP7 DFFHQNx1 measures 1.095 fJ/cycle against the Nangate45 DFF_X1's 3.626, a ratio of 0.302 where the submission assumed 0.116) and on this repository's own post-route SPEF-extracted clock tree (4.329 mW of clock group against 0.987 mW of raw CK pin load, a 4.39x distribution multiplier where the submission asserted 1.925x), it returns 578 W on an A100 rated at 400 W. It is reported as a CEILING CHECK THAT FAILS. What the A100's TDP actually bounds is the product of flip-flop areal density and enabled fraction, to about 63k/mm2 against the 435k x 0.59 = 257k the bottom-up assumed; that 4x is the honest statement of what is unknown here. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a published or measured clock-network power fraction for a post-2015 clock-gated GPU or accelerator (AccelWattch/GPUWattch-class validated breakdown, or a vendor statement). Range 3e-11 to 1.6e-10 spans ~12% (an aggressively gated part at a memory-bound decode step, XScale's 17% being the cited low outlier) to 45%, the top of the published band.
clock_energy_j_per_mm2_per_cycle.source: NVIDIA Ampere architecture whitepaper, die area / TDP / clock table for P100 (610 mm2, 300 W, 1480 MHz, 16FF+) and GV100 (815 mm2, 300 W, 1530 MHz, 12FFN), verified verbatim ; the 20-45% clock-network power fraction band from Dobberpuhl 1992, Restle 2001 and Donno 2004, which could not be re-fetched and is the single load-bearing input

logic.note: 1.0 by definition: clock_energy_j_per_mm2_per_cycle is calibrated on a GPU's whole-die TDP density, and a GPU die is the reference clocked-logic region. Compute, interconnect, HBM PHY and overhead area all carry this multiplier. HBM and SerDes PHY is explicitly NOT set to zero: the argument that its energy is already inside energy.hbm_j_per_byte is wrong, because that term is a per-byte access energy and carries no idle PHY or controller floor.

rom_array.note: 0.15 -- a mask-ROM array's clocked leaf count per mm2 against a logic region's. VERIFIER'S CAUTION CARRIED, AND IT IS THE REASON THE RANGE REACHES 0.5: 0.15 was derived from a LEAF COUNT, but the measured post-route decomposition in this repository shows distribution -- largely wire, whose length is set by AREA and not by leaf count -- at ~3.4x the leaf pin load. Array-region clock power should therefore scale SUB-LINEARLY with leaf density, so 0.15 is likely optimistic for the ROM side and its low end needs a wire argument rather than a latch count. This multiplier and power.fabric_clock_hz multiply, and together they set the W/mm2 asymmetry between the two sides of the comparison this study exists to make, so they are swept jointly and never asserted.
rom_array.source: no published clock-network power for a mask-ROM or compute-in-ROM array; leaf-count argument against the measured wire-dominated distribution at rtl/build/implementation_campaign (post-route, SPEF-extracted)

sram_array.note: 0.15, the same class as a ROM array and for the same reason: an SRAM macro's clocked elements are its periphery -- decoders, sense-amp timing, output latches -- and not a flip-flop field over the bitcell area. Swept 0.05-0.5 jointly with the ROM multiplier and the fabric clock.
sram_array.source: no vendor SRAM macro clock-power breakdown published

clocked_idle_floor_w_per_device.note: 50 W per device of traffic-independent power, applied as a FLOOR on the enumerated static terms and not as an addend -- static power is max(leakage + clock + memory-interface idle, this) -- because leakage and clock ARE most of the physics inside a measured clocked-idle reading and adding both would double-count it. VERIFIER-CORRECTED, from 52 W and, more importantly, on SCOPE: the submission named this gpu_device_fixed_overhead_w and charged it to GPU-class devices only, which is the same class of error as a fitted multiplier and harder to see -- the evidence assembled for it says the floor is clock distribution plus memory-interface clocking on a large clocked die, and a compute-in-ROM part at 815 mm2 with a clocked ROM array and SRAM KV has both. It is charged to BOTH sides here. The value is the mean of four parts' clocked-idle fraction of TDP applied to 400 W: H100 SXM 72.5 W of 700 W = 10.357% (measured, NREL-class facility study); A100 SXM ~50 W of 400 W = 12.5%; B200 140 W of 1000 W = 14.0%; RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 77.03 W of 600 W = 12.84%, which is EXECUTED HERE and is the artifact named above. The submission's 84.6 W reading was REFUTED as an instrumentation artifact -- it averaged a window 4-10 s after a 411 W load stopped, which straddles the decay tail (t+0 s = 116.72 W, t+5 s = 76.95 W in the committed trace) -- and the replicated steady clocked-idle state is 77.03 W across 22 samples at 2610 MHz SM / 13365 MHz memory, util 0. Note what 'clocked' means: the same board at a genuinely idle P-state drops to 7.8 W median, so this is the floor for a device that is up and serving, not a power-gated one. Two caveats the submission hid: the two 'methods' were one, because the low-bandwidth sweep points were produced by duty-cycling and so return clocked-idle power by construction; and the P8 decomposition drops the memory clock 33x at the same time as the SM clock, so roughly 30 W of the 69 W delta is the memory subsystem, which is why memory_interface_idle_w_per_stack is a separate term. The published cross-check is independent and close: SC'25 Table 2 measures P_const = 54 W for the A100 (72 W GH200, 88 W MI250X GCD, 69 W MI300A). The 100 W upper end the submission proposed was REJECTED -- the A100's 100 W Min Power Limit is the lowest cap the driver will enforce, a policy floor and not a consumption measurement. The defensible top is the clocked-and-issuing figure, 80 W.
clocked_idle_floor_w_per_device.source: Executed on this machine: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, 600 W, 1,141 nvidia-smi samples, artifact committed at results/roofline/gpu_clocked_idle_floor.json. Published legs: Vercellino et al., Measurement of Generative AI Workload Power Profiles for Whole-Facility Data Center Infrastructure Planning, arXiv:2604.07345 (2026), Appendix A, 'each idle GPU spent 72.5 W on average' on 700 W H100 SXM ; Measuring the Energy of Data Movement on Modern GPU Systems, SC'25, doi:10.1145/3712285.3759815, Table 2 P_const = 54 W for the A100, as the independent cross-check

fabric_clock_hz.note: 1.0 GHz for a modelled design that has no published clock. THIS IS A MANDATORY COMPANION TO THE CLOCK TERM, not an extra: clock_energy_j_per_mm2_per_cycle has units of J per mm2 per CYCLE, there was no clock frequency anywhere in this file or in roofline.py, and applying the term without one is impossible. It is also NOT new to the model, only newly visible -- the latency block already reasons at '32 stages at a 1 GHz fabric clock' and 'a few cycles at a ~1 GHz fabric clock' without ever stating the clock as an input. The modelled ROM side's clock power is exactly linear in this, and it multiplies with clock_region_multiplier to set the W/mm2 asymmetry between the two sides of the comparison, so the two are swept together. Sweep 0.5-2.0 GHz.
fabric_clock_hz.source: no clock published for any mask-ROM or compute-in-ROM inference die; Taalas publishes no microarchitecture and no frequency

gpu_logic_area_fraction.note: 0.6 of a published GPU die is standard-cell logic; the remaining 0.4 is on-die SRAM, register files, HBM PHY and analogue, and is charged at the SRAM leakage density instead. This model does not allocate a published part's floorplan -- its area is stated for the iso-area comparison, not solved -- so the ONE number needed to apply a per-mm2-of-logic leakage density to a die it did not floorplan is stated here rather than hidden. 0.6 x 826 = 496 mm2 of A100 logic, which is the verifier's own independent estimate of ~500 mm2. Sweep 0.4-0.8: at 0.4 the A100's leakage is 21.5 W and at 0.8 it is 41.4 W, so this parameter is worth about 20 W on a 400 W part. It does not touch the modelled ROM designs, whose regions come from a solved area split.
gpu_logic_area_fraction.source: no vendor floorplan published for any datacentre GPU die; an A100 spends area on HBM PHY, 40 MB of L2, register files and schedulers that a standard-cell leakage density must not be charged over

memory_interface_idle_w_per_stack.note: 2.8 W per HBM stack of traffic-independent DRAM device, PHY and controller power -- standby, refresh and an up-and-trained interface -- charged whether or not a byte moves. The submitted companion to the HBM energy term was filed as `measured` at 3.7 W/stack with a range of 3.27-4.27 and BOTH WERE REFUTED. The grade could not stand: its only source is an anonymous artifact-evaluation drop for a paper still under review -- no authors, no venue, no DOI -- and this file's own vocabulary reserves `measured` for fabricated silicon in a peer-reviewed venue. The range was false precision: both endpoints were the same 6.40 W measurement times two similar ratios, so they could not disagree. The honest interval is 1.2 W (DRAM device standby plus refresh, capacity-scaled from real HBM2 stack IDD2/IDD3N1 measurements of 272/246 mA at 1.2 V after subtracting a per-chip no-HBM baseline) to 6.40 W (a measured H200 memory-rail idle per stack, if HBM2e's subsystem idle is no lower than HBM3e's) -- a 5x band whose geometric centre is 2.8. This term is why clocked_idle_floor_w_per_device is a floor and not an addend: on the A100 the two describe overlapping physics, and SC'25's published P_const of 54 W is the whole traffic-independent draw that both are estimating. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: an Ampere-generation memory-rail measurement (Ampere does not expose the field), a vendor HBM2e stack IDD specification, or A100 baseboard rail telemetry.
memory_interface_idle_w_per_stack.source: HBM2 stack IDD2/IDD3N1/IDD5B measurements and an H200 memory-rail idle reading, both from the CMU-SAFARI/HBM-Power artifact drop (2026) for a paper under review -- no venue, no DOI, so this cannot be graded above `assumed` ; cross-checked against Measuring the Energy of Data Movement on Modern GPU Systems, SC'25, doi:10.1145/3712285.3759815, Table 2

power.purpose: Power a machine spends whether or not a byte moves. Before this block the model counted memory bytes and multiply-accumulates and nothing else, so it gave 54.21 W for an A100 against a published 400 W and 27.04 W for a Taalas HC1 against a published 200-250 W, and -- because step_time = raw_step_time x thermal_scale is the only path from power to any other quantity -- thermal_scale was exactly 1.0 at all 11,747 feasible points and no rate in the study depended on the energy model at all. Every term here is charged PER MM2 PER SECOND against the area split, not against traffic, which is what makes the thermal limit capable of binding. EVERY TERM IN THIS BLOCK WAS ADVERSARIALLY VERIFIED AND EVERY ONE WAS SENT BACK: the values below are the verifiers' corrections, not the submissions, and each note says which way the correction moved. Two of the corrections move power UP and two move it DOWN; none of them was chosen with a gate in view.

logic.note: 0.06 W per mm2 of STANDARD-CELL (logic) region at a 7 nm-class node, at 0.70-0.75 V and 85-105 C junction, on a mix weighted toward RVT. THE UNIT IS LOAD-BEARING AND WAS THE SUBMISSION'S worst defect: it is per mm2 of standard-cell region, NOT per mm2 of die, so on a part that is mostly array this term is charged over the logic only. VERIFIER-CORRECTED, 2x UP from the submitted 0.03. The chain is: an executed ASAP7 place-and-route base of 0.74e-3 W/mm2 of 100%-filled cell area at 25 C/0.70 V typical (from this repository's own results/physical_abi3/asap7 metadata, cross-checked three ways against the liberty's 1 pW leakage unit and against real-scale ASAP7 cell areas), times a threshold-flavour mix, a temperature factor and a voltage factor. The correction is in the threshold ladder: the submission put RELATIVE per-flavour offsets (SLVT 0, LVT 0.071, RVT 0.142 V) inside an exponential that needs the ABSOLUTE saturation threshold, and a device with Vth = 0 is not off. That ladder predicts a 25->100 C ratio of 12.69x at typical/nominal, which is BELOW the 13.82x ASAP7's own SS liberty measures at a slower process AND a lower voltage -- impossible. Re-anchoring to absolute Vth_sat (RVT 0.24, LVT 0.169, SLVT 0.098 V, the lowest ladder clearing that floor) moves the combined mix x T x V factor from 14.8 to 25.3 at the low end and 62.4 to 114.8 at the point. The submission's structural claim that leakier flavours scale less steeply, so mix and temperature partly cancel, is separately FALSIFIED by the same library: measured INVx1 FF/TT ratios are 0.638 / 0.546 / 0.646 across RVT/LVT/SLVT -- flat and non-monotonic -- where the model needs a 1.5x spread. The high end 0.20 is CAPPED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY THE CHAIN: the chain's own 40/40/20 mix at 105 C and 0.85 V gives 0.43 W/mm2, which is 86% of thermal.cooling_limit_w_per_mm2 and is not physical for a shipping part; 0.19-0.20 is where an A100 lands at ~39% of TDP, the top of ReGate's measured 30-72% static-power band. Grade stays `assumed` and correctly so: ASAP7 is a predictive academic PDK, no datacentre die's Vt mix is published anywhere, and the absolute threshold ladder is inferred from Ioff-per-micron rather than read off a datasheet. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a foundry N7/N6 leakage-per-mm2 figure at a stated PVT, or an ASAP7 SRAM-flavour and LVT/SLVT SS liberty.
logic.source: ASAP7 7.5-track predictive PDK NLDM libraries (RVT/LVT/SLVT TT and SS corners) and this repository's executed ASAP7 place-and-route leakage at results/physical_abi3/asap7/add_bf16_sram_engine/pnr_artifacts/metadata.json ; ReGate, MICRO 2025, arXiv:2508.02536, which reports static power at 30-72% of NPU energy

rom_array.note: ZERO, DELIBERATELY, AND THIS IS AN UNDER-CHARGE ON THE ROM SIDE. The submitted companion of 0.006 W/mm2 of array was REFUTED AND REJECTED: the paragraph that derived the SRAM companion completely -- bits/mm2, off-device count, per-cell current, a 64 MB cross-check -- gave the ROM companion no cell density, no device count and no current, and 0.006 is the floor of its own reconstructed 0.006-0.03 bracket with nothing shown. Reconstructing it from this file's own primitives (24.07 Mbit/mm2 usable SRAM, rom.cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio 0.2, rom.array_efficiency 0.70 against sram.array_efficiency 0.65, giving ~130 Mbit/mm2, with one off device per NOR mask-ROM cell against 3-4 in a 6T) gives 0.006-0.03 W/mm2, which is recorded as range_high so a reader can sweep it. It is held at zero rather than at that reconstruction because a companion nobody derived is not evidence. THE DIRECTION IS THE REASON THIS IS SAFE TO SHIP: the ROM array is most of a compute-in-ROM die, so charging it zero leakage makes the modelled ROM power LOWER and the Taalas HC1 power gate's residual LARGER. At the reconstruction's high end it would add roughly 18 W to HC1 -- reported as a sensitivity in the study, never as the value.
rom_array.source: no derivation survived verification; bracket reconstructed from rom.cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio and rom.array_efficiency in this file against the verified SRAM companion

sram_array.note: 0.005 W per mm2 of SRAM ARRAY at a 7 nm-class node. This companion's chain VERIFIED and is carried at the verifier's value, one third below the 0.015 that the same submission's 'of array' companion implied. 0.65 array efficiency over a 0.027 um2 N7 6T bitcell is 24.07 Mbit/mm2 of usable cells; at 0.05-1.0 nA of off current per cell and 0.8 V that is 0.96-19.3 mW/mm2, and the point sits at the geometric-centre end of it. Cross-check that reproduces: 537 Mbit at that density is 22.3 mm2 and 0.021-0.43 W. Charged over SRAM array area only -- the KV store on a ROM part, and the non-logic share of a published GPU die.
sram_array.source: TSMC N7 0.027 um2 6T HD bitcell (this file, nodes.N7) at sram.array_efficiency, times a per-cell off current of 0.05-1.0 nA at 0.8 V; no vendor SRAM macro leakage published for the target arrays

purpose: Graded technology primitives for the area-constrained roofline model. Every entry is a primitive input; capacities, bandwidths and compute roofs are derived from these by src/opentallas/roofline.py and are never stated here.

hbm_stacks.note: five active HBM2e stacks on the 80GB part

clock_frequency_hz.note: NVIDIA publishes no B200 clock in any first-party document; 1.965 GHz is the commonly cited boost figure and is graded `assumed` rather than `published` for exactly that reason. Sweep 1.4-2.0 GHz. It enters only power.clock_energy_j_per_mm2_per_cycle and no rate depends on it.
clock_frequency_hz.source: no first-party NVIDIA statement of a B200 clock frequency

die_area_mm2.note: two reticle-limited dies in one package, ~1600 mm2 of silicon per package

dies_per_package.note: counted per package for iso-area comparison

die_area_mm2.note: wafer-scale die, used only as the wafer area and fabric anchor

batch_size.note: The figure is quoted per user, so batch is modelled as 1 for the anchor. On this model's ROM weight path the anchor rate is batch-independent for a dense model, so the assumption does not move the anchor; it does move the aggregate throughput and the SRAM KV area.
batch_size.source: not published by Taalas; checked taalas.com, CNX Software, Wavect and Kaitchup

execution_format.note: canonical execution format 'w4a8'. Taalas publishes a custom 3-bit base type with a 3/6-bit mixture for weights; the activation width is not published and 8 bits is assumed. A model-specific ASIC freezes one datapath at manufacture, so the checkpoint's released BF16 arithmetic is NOT what this part executes and must not be priced at the BF16 roof.

output_tokens.note: 1K output sequence length; the quoted rate is sustained to a final context of 2048 tokens

power_w.note: Reported around 250 W per PCIe card; a ten-card server is quoted at 2.5 kW. Taalas states no TDP directly, and the figures in circulation put the card between 200 and 250 W, so the range is the published BAND and the power gate reports against both ends of it. The value stays at the top of the band, which is the harder end for a model that lands below it, and quoting the harder end as the headline is the reading that does not flatter the model.

published_tokens_s_per_user.note: 16,960 tokens/s per user on Llama 3.1 8B at 1k input / 1k output. Every figure is self-run by Taalas; there is no MLPerf or third-party measurement, and the batch size is stated nowhere. The rounded '17k' on the product page is the same number.

weight_amortization.note: HC1 is a compute-in-ROM part: Bajic describes one transistor storing four bits and doing the multiply for them. Llama-3.1-8B is dense, so every token engages the whole array and per_stream and per_region are the same machine here. Evaluating the anchor as 'batched' would model a MAC array the part does not have, which matters now that the floorplan depends on the policy.
weight_amortization.source: Taalas publishes no batch size and no microarchitecture

weight_bits_per_parameter.note: Taalas publishes a custom 3-bit base type with a mixture of 3-bit and 6-bit parameters but no mix ratio. 3.5 bits/parameter is the stated point; sweep 3.0 to 6.0.

area_mm2.note: Taalas HC1 die area, used as the reticle-class chip area for array designs so the array and the anchor are the same unit of silicon

array_efficiency.note: Taken above the SRAM array efficiency because a ROM macro carries no write drivers and no write-assist circuitry. Sweep 0.60 to 0.80.
array_efficiency.source: no published mask-ROM macro floorplan at a leading node

cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio.note: A contact/via-programmed NOR mask-ROM bit is one transistor with no write port, no write assist and no write redundancy, against a 6T SRAM bit. 1/6 to 1/4 brackets the plausible cell-area ratio; 1/5 is the stated point. This is the single most load-bearing assumption in the ROM capacity chain and must be swept.
cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio.source: no fabricated leading-node mask-ROM bitcell has been published for this program

cim_cell_area_multiplier.note: area of a compute-in-ROM cell relative to a storage-only mask-ROM cell. A compute-in-ROM cell carries a pass transistor and the product-line wiring that lets it select one pre-computed partial product, on top of the via programming that stores its bits. Taalas describes one transistor per 4-bit parameter doing both, so the multiplier is small but cannot be 1.0. This is the second most load-bearing assumption in this file after the ROM-to-SRAM cell ratio, and it decides the storage-versus-compute-in-ROM comparison.
cim_cell_area_multiplier.source: no published compute-in-ROM bitcell at any node

cim_precompute_area_fraction.note: fraction of die area a compute-in-ROM part spends on the pre-computation block that forms every product of one activation with the small weight alphabet. At 3-bit weights that is 8 values, built from shifts and carry-save adders, and it replaces the dedicated MAC array entirely. Small by construction, which is the point of the architecture.
cim_precompute_area_fraction.source: derived shape only: 2^b shift-add units per activation-broadcast region

cross_checks.name: fabricated 28 nm hybrid SRAM/ROM-CIM macro density
cross_checks.note: 8.928 Mbit/mm2 at 28 nm on fabricated silicon. It is a compute-in-memory macro, so its density is a lower bound on a pure storage ROM array. Scaled to N6 by the same published bitcell-area ratio this model uses elsewhere (4.70x) it gives 42.0 Mbit/mm2 = 5.2 MB/mm2, against the 16.2 MB/mm2 this model derives for a storage-only array -- consistent with a CIM macro spending most of its area on compute. Cross-check only; not an input.

cross_checks.name: 3D-METRO transistorless 3D-metal ROM density
cross_checks.note: 20.7 MB/mm2 from a simulated evaluation, not fabricated silicon. Upper cross-check on the 16.2 MB/mm2 this model derives at N6 for a planar array. Cross-check only; not an input.

anchor_node_sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: TSMC 28 nm HKMG high-density 6T SRAM bitcell, 0.127 um2. Used to scale the 28 nm ROM-CIM read-bandwidth density to the target node by published array-density ratio.

macro_area_mm2.note: simulated, not fabricated; carried over from configs/hardware/technology_inputs.json

operations_per_weight.note: one stored weight participates in one multiply-add per dense matrix-vector pass
operations_per_weight.source: definition, not a publication: one stored weight participates in one multiply and one add per dense matrix-vector pass, and the FLOP convention counts those as two operations. Regraded from `published` -- nobody published this, it is how the unit is defined, and calling a definition a publication is the same error class as calling a reading of an implementation a derivation.

read_bandwidth_scaling_rule.note: Read-bandwidth density is scaled by (anchor-node bitcell area / target-node bitcell area): the same macro throughput in proportionally less area. No clock-frequency bonus is applied on top. For 28 nm -> N6 this ratio is 4.70x, which corresponds to an effective density-scaling exponent of 1.005 on (28/6) -- the wire/periphery-limited CONSERVATIVE end of the 1.0-2.0 bracket documented in src/opentallas/technology.py. src/opentallas/technology.py documents 1.0-2.0 as the plausible exponent bracket; this rule sits at its conservative end.
read_bandwidth_scaling_rule.source: published 6T HD bitcell areas at 28 nm and at the target node

array_efficiency.note: bitcell area divided by total macro area including decoders, sense amplifiers, write drivers and redundancy. Published foundry macros land between 0.55 and 0.75; sweep that range.
array_efficiency.source: no vendor macro floorplan published for the target arrays

read_bandwidth_anchor.attribution_note: The derived density is charged against WHOLE-die area but is then applied only to the SRAM array area of a modelled design. WSE-2's SRAM occupies a minority of its die, so this is a conservative (low) bandwidth density for an SRAM array.

scaling_rule.note: as the ROM rule; the anchor is at N7 so the N7 and N6 ratios are 1.00
scaling_rule.source: published 6T HD bitcell areas at N7 and at the target node

cooling_limit_w_per_mm2.note: A100 SXM dissipates 400 W over an 826 mm2 die, 0.484 W/mm2, rounded to 0.50. Cross-checks: Taalas HC1 at a reported 250 W over 815 mm2 is 0.31 W/mm2, and a 15-23 kW wafer over 46,225 mm2 is 0.32-0.50 W/mm2.

units: areas mm^2 unless a field name says um2; bytes and bits decimal SI; times seconds; energy joules

reticle_regions.note: 46,225 mm2 divided by the 815 mm2 reticle field; sets the on-wafer pipeline hop count
